title: OpenAI claims a Navier–Stokes proof, then walks into a credit fight
subtitle: An unreleased model ran ~10,000 parallel agents for 88 hours to construct a finite-time blowup — verified in Lean — but an NYU mathematician alleges the effort drew on his private Codex-hosted notes.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI announced on September 8, 2026, that an unreleased model had constructed a proof relating to Navier–Stokes, one of the Clay Institute's seven Millennium Prize Problems. The claimed result is a finite-time blowup: a smooth three-dimensional fluid configuration in which a vortex tightens and spins ever faster and the equations governing the flow break down in finite time, while the fluid's kinetic energy remains bounded throughout. The proof was verified in Lean and produced by roughly 10,000 agent instances working in parallel over 88 hours. OpenAI dated the work as beginning September 1 after the lab "heard a rumor" that human progress was near.

Within hours the announcement was in dispute. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at NYU, publicly alleged that OpenAI's system may have drawn on his private research notes stored inside Codex. OpenAI's response is that its work on the problem began after it heard about parallel human efforts by Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic; that OpenAI completed its own proof and Lean verification by September 6; and that when it then contacted the two researchers to propose a joint announcement, it learned their result addressed the forced Euler equations — a related but distinct problem — rather than Navier–Stokes proper. Independent verification of the Lean artifact is now the ballgame.

The context is that formal verification in Lean has quietly become the accepted currency of AI-generated math over 2026. Anthropic's Fermat's Last Theorem work earlier this month used it, DeepMind's IMO agent work uses it, and the Terry Tao–led community has been building the Mathlib scaffolding that makes it possible. What OpenAI is claiming is a step change in scale: not a lemma or a competition problem, but a Millennium result — the kind of thing that carries a $1 million Clay prize and reshapes a field. Even if the proof holds up, the credit dispute is going to force the AI-math community to write clearer rules for what constitutes independent discovery when the model has read the private notebooks of everyone working on the problem.

Takeaway for learners: two things are becoming true at once. First, machine-checkable mathematics — proofs that compile in Lean rather than proofs that read well — is the new bar, because it is the only bar an AI's contribution can clear without human trust. Second, if you work in AI-adjacent research fields, your notes are now part of the training and retrieval surface of the model you use to write them; the boundary between "my private work" and "model context" is being litigated in real time. Both changes will matter more than the specific fluid-dynamics result — and the profession's response over the next six months will set the norms.
